definition: Handwriting recognition (HWR), also known as handwritten text recognition (HTR), is the ability of a computer to receive and interpret intelligible handwritten input from sources such as paper documents, photographs, touch-screens and other devices.
details: The image of the written text may be sensed "off line" from a piece of paper by optical scanning (optical character recognition) or intelligent word recognition. Alternatively, the movements of the pen tip may be sensed "on line", for example by a pen-based computer screen surface, a generally easier task as there are more clues available. A handwriting recognition system handles formatting, performs correct segmentation into characters, and finds the most possible words.

explainer.lead: Handwriting recognition turns writing made by a person into text a computer can interpret. It makes handwritten paper documents, photographs, and pen or touch-screen input useful in digital systems.

tiers.eli5: It is like teaching a computer to read someone's handwriting instead of only printed letters. The computer can look at a picture of the writing, or watch the pen move as someone writes. It then works out the characters and chooses the words that make the most sense.
tiers.practitioner: Applications receive either offline images obtained by scanning paper or online pen-tip movements captured on a writing surface. Processing must address formatting and character segmentation before selecting the most likely words. Online recognition is generally easier because pen movement provides additional clues; image quality and incorrect segmentation can complicate offline input.
tiers.paperLevel: Handwriting recognition maps an input X to intelligible handwritten text, where X is an offline text image or an online sequence of pen-tip movements. A system performs formatting, character segmentation, and selection of the most probable words. Offline input provides fewer clues than online input, making the former generally harder.

explainer.example: A scanned handwritten note containing the word “milk” enters as an offline image. The system segments the handwritten characters, evaluates the possible words, and returns “milk” as interpreted text.

usedIn.name: Paper document processing
usedIn.detail: Optical scanning supplies offline images of handwritten text for recognition.

usedIn.name: Photograph transcription
usedIn.detail: Handwriting appearing in photographs can be interpreted as computer-readable input.

usedIn.name: Touch-screen input
usedIn.detail: A touch-screen can capture handwriting for interpretation by a recognition system.

usedIn.name: Pen-based computing
usedIn.detail: A pen-sensitive screen records pen-tip movements for online recognition.

explainer.intuition: The central idea is to recover readable writing from either its appearance or the motion that produced it. Pen motion offers extra evidence, while a scanned page leaves the system to interpret the finished image.
howItWorks: Receive handwriting from paper, a photograph, a touch-screen, or another device.
For offline input, sense the written image through optical scanning; for online input, record pen-tip movements.
Handle formatting and divide the writing into characters.
Find the most likely words and produce intelligible interpreted text.
explainer.whyItMatters: It allows handwritten material to serve as computer input instead of remaining only marks on paper or a screen. Supporting both images and pen movements makes it useful across document and interactive-device settings.
misconceptions: It is not limited to scanned paper: online systems can interpret pen-tip movements as writing occurs.
Offline and online recognition are not equally easy; online recognition generally has more clues and is therefore easier.
